entities.name: Thomas Grenville
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thomas Grenville (1755–1846) was a distinguished British statesman, diplomat, and, most significantly, a renowned bibliophile whose magnificent library fundamentally enriched the British Museum. Born into the powerful Grenville-Temple family, he served three decades as a Member of Parliament and held various ministerial posts, including First Lord of the Admiralty during the Ministry of All the Talents (1806-1807). However, his enduring legacy transcends his political career, resting instead on his profound passion for collecting rare books, which culminated in one of the most significant private bequests to a national institution in British history.

Educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, Grenville entered Parliament in 1780, representing constituencies such as Buckingham and Buckinghamshire. His political appointments included a diplomatic mission to Paris in 1782 to negotiate peace with the fledgling United States, and later, President of the Board of Control (1807). Yet, throughout his public life, Grenville meticulously assembled a personal library of over 20,000 volumes. His collection was distinguished by its scholarly focus, encompassing classical literature, voyages and travels, incunabula (books printed before 1501), and early editions across various subjects, reflecting an unparalleled discernment and commitment to the history of printing.

Grenville’s most profound impact came posthumously with his bequest of 20,240 volumes to the British Museum in 1846. This monumental gift, valued at an estimated £50,000, instantly transformed the Museum's holdings, elevating it to a premier international center for rare book scholarship. The 'Grenville Library' housed within the British Library today, includes irreplaceable items like a Gutenberg Bible, a Shakespeare First Folio, and numerous unique early printed works, providing an invaluable resource for historians and researchers worldwide.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Thomas Grenville's bequest of over 20,000 rare books to the British Museum transformed its capacity as a research institution, providing invaluable resources for scholars globally for centuries to come. His act set a precedent for public cultural endowment, shaping the future of national libraries.
